p: In the winter of nineteen hundred and one, a French expedition digging at the ancient city of Susa, in Persia, found three great pieces of black stone which, joined together, made a pillar a little more than two metres high, that is about seven feet. At its top was carved an image of a king standing respectfully before a seated god, who hands him the emblems of authority. Below, covering the pillar on every side, were nearly three hundred laws, written in cuneiform in the Babylonian language. It was the code of Hammurabi, king of Babylon, who reigned about one thousand seven hundred and fifty years before Christ. The pillar had been carried to Susa as plunder by an invading king some six hundred years after it was made. It stands now in the Museum of the Louvre in Paris. I record these facts as the Encyclopaedia gives them, with the professional envy of a man who will not live to see the stone.

Hammurabi was the sixth king of a dynasty of Amorites, a people who had come into Mesopotamia from the west, and who ruled at first only the modest city of Babylon. In a reign of some forty-two years, by war and by diplomacy, he made himself master of all southern Mesopotamia, and Babylon, from a small town, became the greatest city of the world, a position it held, on and off, for over a thousand years.

His code was not the first. The Encyclopaedia records older collections of laws in Sumerian, the earliest of them made under Ur-Nammu, king of Ur, some three hundred years before. But Hammurabi's is the longest and best preserved, and it was copied by the scribes of Mesopotamia as a classic for a thousand years after his death. In its prologue and epilogue the king explains that the gods called him to cause justice to appear in the land, to destroy the wicked and the evil, so that the strong might not oppress the weak. He invites any man who has a grievance to come and stand before his image and have the stone read to him, so that he may understand his case and his heart may be eased.

The laws themselves are arranged as a series of cases, each beginning with the word if: if a man does this, then that shall be done to him. They cover a remarkable range of life: theft and robbery, the hiring of labourers and oxen, the rents of fields and the repair of canals, debts and deposits, marriage, divorce, adoption and inheritance, the fees of physicians and the responsibility of builders, and the treatment of slaves.

Many of the penalties are severe. The famous principle of an eye for an eye, which you know from the Book of Exodus, appears here centuries before; if a man puts out the eye of another man of his own rank, his own eye shall be put out. If a builder builds a house so badly that it falls and kills the owner, the builder shall be put to death; if it kills the owner's son, the builder's son shall be put to death. Death is prescribed for many offences, including some kinds of theft. Some cases were to be decided by ordeal: a person accused of sorcery was to leap into the river, and if the river overwhelmed him, he was guilty, and if he came out safe, he was innocent, and his accuser was put to death.

But I would warn you against reading the code only for its cruelties, which are the cruelties of every ancient society and many modern ones. The principle of the eye for an eye was, in its time, a limit on vengeance, not an incitement to it: one eye for one eye, and not a life for an eye, nor a blood-feud between families for generations. And the code is in other respects humane. A wife whose husband is taken captive may remarry if she has no means of support. A debtor who has sold his family into servitude must have them freed after three years. A widow keeps her dowry. The weak are, in principle at least, protected.

What a modern reader notices at once is that the law is not the same for everyone. The code distinguishes three ranks of person: the free man of the upper class, a lesser kind of free person, and the slave. The penalty for injuring each is different. To knock out the tooth of a man of one's own rank costs one's own tooth; to knock out the tooth of a commoner costs a fine in silver. The idea that all men are equal before the law, which we in England like to suppose we have always possessed, and which in fact we acquired slowly and painfully over many centuries, would have seemed absurd to Hammurabi. Every society, he would have said, has its ranks, and justice is to give each rank its due.

The scholars of the future have raised a doubt which I find very interesting. Among the many thousands of legal documents that survive from Babylon, the contracts, the records of trials and the letters of judges, hardly any refer to Hammurabi's code. Judges do not cite it. It may be, therefore, that it was not a code in our sense, a book of rules to be applied in court, but rather a monument: a royal proclamation of the king's justice, a model of wise judgements, meant to impress the gods and posterity as much as to guide the magistrates. If so, it has succeeded admirably. The gods have not recorded their opinion, but posterity has never forgotten it.

I find in it, above all, the first clear expression of an idea that runs through the rest of this history: that the power of the ruler is justified only by justice, and that justice must be written down, so that the weak may know what is owed to them. That idea has been betrayed in every age. It has never been entirely forgotten.
